annotations.text:
The desktop question was never "the same page, wider" — tlv-day.jpg is 679px native and tlv-night.jpg is 416px, so a full-bleed 1440px header would upscale one 2.1x and the other 3.5x. Never. So every board here keeps the settled header exactly as approved (masthead, zmanim ribbon, mode toggle) with the photograph at its true size along the leading edge and a painted gradient carrying the rest — and spends the extra 1440px width on a genuinely different BODY, not a bigger photograph.

All three use real data from the running app today (ט״ו אלול תשפ״ו, שקיעה 19:10): the same 15–16 Ramat Aviv shuls, the same חב״ד tag on תומכי תמימים, the same unpublished-offset row on הרמב״ם, the same one real relative offset on לכלל ישראל (שקיעה פחות 20). Nothing here is lorem.

Approved mobile boards sit to the right for direct comparison — none of these three contradict them, only the header repeats and the body changes.

1 · THE LUACH (הלוח) — one dense table across the full width, like a printed זמנים לוח pinned in a shul lobby. The "next minyan" hero is just the table's own top row, picked out by a rule, not a different kind of object. Best for scanning all 15 shuls fast.

Tradeoff: the coldest of the three — no floating hero card, nothing that visually says "same family as the mobile site" without the header's help.

2 · THREE RIBBONS — שחרית / מנחה / ערבית as three parallel columns, a literal Bauhaus ribbon-window composition. Compares services at a glance instead of filtering to one.

The payoff is not staged: ערבית is real data from the app right now — 0 Ramat Aviv shuls publish an evening time — so that column is drawn genuinely empty, using the same quiet unknown-row language CLAUDE.md specifies, just at the scale of a whole column. It is the exact gap the project names, made visible.

Tradeoff: a shul can appear in more than one column (לכלל ישראל is in both שחרית and מנחה here) — the opposite problem from the Luach board, where every shul appears exactly once.

3 · THE HORIZON — a continuous horizontal ribbon plotting the day itself, נץ to צאת read right-to-left, under a mobile-style card grid reflowed to three columns. The most literally Bauhaus of the three (a ribbon window, not a metaphor for one) and the closest to mobile's own warmth.

Only KNOWN, published times get a tick — an unpublished בזמן has no honest position to plot, so the eight Mincha unknowns are named only as a count beside the band, never guessed onto the line.

Tradeoff: safest and most familiar of the three — the card grid is barely a decision, just mobile's card reflowed wider — so nearly the whole argument rides on whether the strip reads at a glance.

Photo moved into the header band, two ways. Each artboard has a 'bleed' toggle.

OFF = B: the photograph sits sharp on the leading edge at its true size, a painted gradient carrying the rest. Night is an exact 1:1 pixel crop.

ON = A: the photograph fills the whole header, upscaled 1.9x (day) or 3.1x (night), blurred to hide it.

Turn A on and look at what is left of the photograph.

The photographic direction in two modes, using your own photographs.

The switch is driven by the clock, not a preference — the site turns dark at real shkia and light again at netz, the same way the Hebrew date rolls at sunset. The small sun/moon button beside the language switch lets you override it.

No photograph is stretched: every one renders below its native size. The night frame is portrait, so it gets a tall header on mobile and a tall narrow panel on desktop rather than being cropped into a letterbox.

Three directions, each now at phone size (top row) and full desktop width (below).

Built from photographs of the city rather than from architectural theory. Same content everywhere — same shuls, same times, same honest-unknown row — so this is a comparison of visual language.

Flip the Sunset toggle on any artboard.

What the extra width earned, per direction:

Photographic — the image now does two jobs at two scales: a scrimmed panoramic wash behind the masthead, and a crisp unscaled panel where the map placeholder used to be.

Night City — the gradient has room to actually gradate, plus a flat skyline silhouette and a night map with glowing pins.

Day Sea — a real horizon line, and the hero card overlaps the band edge with one curved corner: a balcony breaking a flat facade.

The photograph is real — Tel Aviv at blue hour by Martin Furtschegger, CC BY 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons. Self-hosted, resized to 39KB, credited in the artboard as the licence requires.

Worth weighing: one photograph cannot represent 484 synagogues. Shipping this means either per-shul photography or a rotating set of city shots.
Kept for the record. All five were rejected as not looking like Tel Aviv — the palette is a desaturated version of the real thing.

Photographic with the map restored. The photograph moves entirely to the header band; the map returns to its own slot.

The designer deliberately kept the map as a drawn schematic rather than satellite imagery — its argument being that two photographs would leave the page with no functional layer at all, which is the opposite of what you asked for.
